subject: Stan wish list for Bayesian demography

messages.author: 7d255fb0a802b78d
messages.subject: Stan wish list for Bayesian demography
parts:
Hi Stanners!

One of my research interests is in Bayesian models for population
demography. By that I mean population demographic models that take
uncertainties in the parameter estimates into account, and provide
uncertainties for the model outputs (population growth rate etc.), using
a Bayesian approach. The key reference here is Poole, D. & Raftery, A.
E. Inference for deterministic simulation models: The Bayesian melding
approach Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2000, 95,
1244-1255.

Poole and Raftery use the SIR algorithm to compute posterior densities
for model outputs, however I think it would be EXTREMELY cool to
implement Poole and Raftery's approach in Stan. These population models
are matrix models, which are asymmetric. Analysing the models amounts to
an eigenanalysis of this population projection matrix. Consequently, I
need to be able to calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors for asymmetric
matrices. Could this functionality be added to Stan?

Another feature of the Poole and Raftery approach is that there are TWO
priors on each input and output of the model (this avoids the Borel
paradox). One is the usual subjective prior. The other is the prior
induced on the outputs by the priors on the model inputs. This prior is
obtained by sampling from the input priors and then running them through
the matrix model. Then follows logarithmic pooling of the two priors to
produce a single prior for each output, and then usual Bayesian
inference can be conducted. I'm not sure how to do this in Stan, but I
am willing to try. If anyone has any ideas on how to do it, I'm all ears!

On a lighter note, you can buy Stan Ulam shirts on the Internet!!
http://www.zazzle.com/ulam_fermiac_tee_shirts-235971823213376354

Cheers,

Simon.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Borel paradox and parameterization [was Re: [stan-users] Stan wish list for Bayesian demography]
parts:
I'm trying to get Michael's attention with the new subject.
This is much more up his alley than mine. More below.

On 1/28/14, 2:46 AM, Simon Blomberg wrote:
> Hi Stanners!
>
> One of my research interests is in Bayesian models for population demography. By that I mean population demographic
> models that take uncertainties in the parameter estimates into account, and provide uncertainties for the model outputs
> (population growth rate etc.), using a Bayesian approach. The key reference here is Poole, D. & Raftery, A. E. Inference
> for deterministic simulation models: The Bayesian melding approach Journal of the American Statistical Association,
> 2000, 95, 1244-1255.
>
> Poole and Raftery use the SIR algorithm to compute posterior densities for model outputs, however I think it would be
> EXTREMELY cool to implement Poole and Raftery's approach in Stan. These population models are matrix models, which are
> asymmetric. Analysing the models amounts to an eigenanalysis of this population projection matrix. Consequently, I need
> to be able to calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors for asymmetric matrices. Could this functionality be added to Stan?

Yes, it'd be pretty easy --- there are asymmetric algorithms in the
Eigen package we use. Unless we could work out some analytic
gradients, it'd be relatively slow. How big are the matrices
that need to be decomposed?

> Another feature of the Poole and Raftery approach is that there are TWO priors on each input and output of the model
> (this avoids the Borel paradox). One is the usual subjective prior. The other is the prior induced on the outputs by the
> priors on the model inputs. This prior is obtained by sampling from the input priors and then running them through the
> matrix model.

There's no way to do any kind of across-iteration inference in
Stan. But if it can be expressed as a density, we could do it.

> Then follows logarithmic pooling of the two priors to produce a single prior for each output, and then
> usual Bayesian inference can be conducted. I'm not sure how to do this in Stan, but I am willing to try. If anyone has
> any ideas on how to do it, I'm all ears!

If by putting two priors, you just mean you want to have

theta ~ foo(...);
theta ~ bar(...);

with the interpretation

p(theta|..., ...) = foo(theta|...) * bar(theta|...)

you can just write it as above.

> On a lighter note, you can buy Stan Ulam shirts on the Internet!!
> http://www.zazzle.com/ulam_fermiac_tee_shirts-235971823213376354

Cool --- I'm about to put up a page with Stan t-shirts.
Hopefully in time for our next release.

- Bob

Hmm. This could be a sticking point. The problem is that the induced

as a vector in a second analysis, then randomly sample from that vector?

Yes, it'd be pretty easy --- there are asymmetric algorithms in the
Eigen package we use.  Unless we could work out some analytic
gradients, it'd be relatively slow.  How big are the matrices
that need to be decomposed?

Excellent! I guess a size of ~ 100 would be considered very large. <= 10 would be more common.

There are some results for the derivatives of left/right eigenvalues/vectors but my
is that they’ll be a pain to implement.

Another feature of the Poole and Raftery approach is that there are TWO priors on each input and output of the model
(this avoids the Borel paradox). One is the usual subjective prior. The other is the prior induced on the outputs by the
priors on the model inputs. This prior is obtained by sampling from the input priors and then running them through the
matrix model.

I don’t really understand the model, but I’m not sure the import of the Borel paradox or
how this odd procedure would attempt to “fix” it.  The Borel paradox is one of
misinterpretation, not anything incorrect with probability theory.

Can you provide a reference?

There's no easy way to randomly sample in a Stan model,

I'll let others respond, though, who may understand what

the density and then reading it back in as a vector" --- I take

You could also do that in Stan with:

increment_log_prob(0.5 * (foo_log(theta,...) + bar_log(theta,...)));

I should add an example to the manual of the elastic net prior, which does
the same thing by averaging a normal (L2) and Laplace (L1) prior (regularizer).
I created an issue:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/518

- Bob

On Mon, Jan 27, 2014 at 9:01 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
I'm trying to get Michael's attention with the new subject.
This is much more up his alley than mine.  More below.

On 1/28/14, 2:46 AM, Simon Blomberg wrote:
Hi Stanners!

One of my research interests is in Bayesian models for population demography. By that I mean population demographic
models that take uncertainties in the parameter estimates into account, and provide uncertainties for the model outputs
(population growth rate etc.), using a Bayesian approach. The key reference here is Poole, D. & Raftery, A. E. Inference
for deterministic simulation models: The Bayesian melding approach Journal of the American Statistical Association,
2000, 95, 1244-1255.

Poole and Raftery use the SIR algorithm to compute posterior densities for model outputs, however I think it would be
EXTREMELY cool to implement Poole and Raftery's approach in Stan. These population models are matrix models, which are
asymmetric. Analysing the models amounts to an eigenanalysis of this population projection matrix. Consequently, I need
to be able to calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors for asymmetric matrices. Could this functionality be added to Stan?

Yes, it'd be pretty easy --- there are asymmetric algorithms in the
Eigen package we use.  Unless we could work out some analytic
gradients, it'd be relatively slow.  How big are the matrices
that need to be decomposed?

Asymmetric eigenanalysis would be a bit harder than just wrapping the write Eigen functions.  The eigenvalues and eigenvectors or an asymmetric matrix can be complex.  We'd either need to support complex numbers or, in a pinch, we could return the real and imaginary parts separately but this would become tedious at best.

Cheers,
Marcus
